identity.title: Don't Force the Fit: Bounded Log-Likelihood Loss for Enhanced Reasoning in Large Language Models

problem.claim: SFT must align token-level training with reasoning behavior whose correctness depends on logical validity or final outcomes rather than exact wording.

gap.claim: The abstract identifies a mismatch in standard SFT: strictly fitting every demonstration token can overweight realization-specific or stylistic variation in reasoning tasks.

contributions.claim: Proposes Bounded Log-Likelihood Loss (BLL-Loss), a parameter-free alternative that bounds gradient contributions from low-probability tokens while retaining conventional optimization behavior.
Reports theoretical insights and empirical evaluation of BLL-Loss across model scales and challenging reasoning benchmarks.

stated_novelty.claim: The authors distinguish BLL-Loss as a simple, parameter-free bounded-gradient alternative to standard likelihood training for reasoning alignment.

author_reported_evidence.claim: The authors report that low-probability tokens in reasoning demonstrations often represent realization-specific or stylistic variation, and that reducing their training influence consistently improves reasoning-benchmark generalization.
The authors report improvements in reasoning generalization across diverse model scales and challenging benchmarks, alongside theoretical insights.

narrative_sequence.summary: SFT is presented as central to aligning LLMs with instruction following and task-specific reasoning.
Standard token-level likelihood training implicitly assumes that fitting every expert token produces desired downstream behavior, which may misalign with outcome-based reasoning correctness.
The authors report that low-probability reasoning tokens often encode stylistic or realization-specific variation, and that downweighting them improves generalization.
They introduce BLL-Loss and report theoretical and empirical evidence of improved reasoning generalization across scales and benchmarks.

source_observation.claim: The abstract separates reasoning correctness from exact token realization and links low-probability tokens to stylistic or realization-specific variation.

lessons.interpretation: This suggests framing the training objective around the task’s success criterion rather than treating every demonstrated surface form as equally essential.
lessons.application: When presenting an objective for outcome-based reasoning, explicitly identify which demonstration details may be incidental and explain how the loss limits their influence.
lessons.exception: This framing may be unsuitable when exact wording, token fidelity, or stylistic reproduction is itself the task objective.

unknowns: The abstract does not specify the exact bound, implementation, benchmark names, model sizes, baselines, or quantitative gains.
The reported consistency and improvement conditions are not detailed, so their scope cannot be assessed from the abstract alone.
